title: A model of phototransduction by the human circadian system
central_proposition: The paper proposes a hypothesized model of human circadian phototransduction, integrating known neuroanatomy and physiology, with spectral opponency as a fundamental mechanism, to explain light's effects on the human circadian system.

concept_definitions.name: Circadian phototransduction
concept_definitions.definition: The absolute and spectral sensitivities to light by the human circadian system, measured through melatonin suppression or phase shifting response.

concept_definitions.name: Melanopsin-containing retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs)
concept_definitions.definition: A unique class of mammalian RGCs central to circadian phototransduction that are directly photosensitive and express melanopsin.

concept_definitions.name: Spectral opponency
concept_definitions.definition: Retinal photopigments are combined into a non-additive, spectrally opponent mechanism leading to nocturnal melatonin suppression in humans.

concept_definitions.name: Circadian stimulus (CS)
concept_definitions.definition: The instantaneous circadian stimulus, in weighted irradiance units, that when applied over time produces a given circadian dose-response value.

argument_structure: The argument is built by reviewing existing neuroanatomy, electrophysiology, and psychophysics literature on human circadian phototransduction. These findings are synthesized into a mathematical model that incorporates specific photoreceptor types (rods, L, M, S cones, and ipRGCs) and their interactions, emphasizing spectral opponency and a high threshold mechanism. The model's predictions are then validated against empirical data for nocturnal melatonin suppression and spectral sensitivity.
mechanism_or_causal_logic: The model proposes that circadian phototransduction results from the integration of signals from classical photoreceptors (rods, L, M, S cones) and intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs). Rods establish a high threshold for circadian activation by providing shunting inhibition to ipRGC dendrites via AII amacrine cells. As light levels increase, rod response saturates, reducing inhibition and effectively adding a 'double negative' (positive contribution) to spectral sensitivity. Spectral opponency, primarily through the S cone pathway (b-y system), modulates ipRGC activity: short-wavelength (blue) light from S cone bipolars directly excites ipRGCs via diode-like ON synapses, while long-wavelength (yellow) light from S cone bipolars signals A18 amacrine cells (via diode-like OFF synapses) to decouple rod inhibition. At high light levels and for wavelengths longer than the b-y cross-point (~500 nm), ipRGCs' intrinsic photosensitivity (peak 480 nm) drives the response, free from rod inhibition. For shorter wavelengths, the response is a combination of ipRGC intrinsic activity, S cone excitation, and the loss of rod inhibition.

findings.antecedent: Low light level (scotopic) stimulation to rods
findings.mechanism: Rods set a high threshold for circadian phototransduction through shunting inhibitory AII amacrine cell connections on ipRGC dendrites. ipRGCs can only give a depolarizing ON response, so shunting AII input sets a higher than expected threshold, preventing a measurable response at low light levels.
findings.quote: Low light level (scotopic) stimulation to the rods does not provide a measurable circadian response in humans
findings.empirical_support_cited: Low light level (scotopic) stimulation to the rods does not provide a measurable circadian response in humans [3,53,59,60,62,79,80,106].

findings.mechanism: Rods provide shunting inhibition to ipRGCs via AII amacrine cells. A response is sent to the SCN only when ipRGC excitation overcomes this rod inhibition.
findings.quote: no response can be sent to the SCN until excitation in the ipRGCs exceeds rod inhibition via the AII amacrine cell connections.

findings.antecedent: Short-wavelength (blue) radiation stimulating S cone bipolar
findings.mechanism: The S cone bipolar, exhibiting b-ON spectral opponency, contributes to excitatory depolarization of the ipRGC through a diode-like synapse in the proximal ON layer of the IPL, allowing only depolarizing ON signals to pass.
findings.quote: When the S cone bipolar is stimulated with short-wavelength radiation, it contributes to the excitatory depolarizing response of the ipRGC
findings.empirical_support_cited: The S cone bipolar gives a bivalent depolarizing ON (blue) and hyperpolarizing OFF (yellow) response to light [21].

findings.antecedent: Long-wavelength (yellow) radiation stimulating S cone bipolar
findings.mechanism: The S cone bipolar's hyperpolarizing OFF (yellow) signal is communicated to A18 amacrine cells (via a diode-like synapse allowing only OFF signals), which then 'decouple' AII amacrine cells from ipRGCs, thereby releasing rod inhibition.
findings.quote: the hyperpolarizing OFF signals from the S cone bipolar would be communicated to A18 amacrine cells... to release rod inhibition reaching the ipRGC

findings.antecedent: Rod response saturation (due to increasing light levels)
findings.mechanism: As rods saturate, their inhibitory effect on ipRGCs via AII amacrine cells diminishes, leading to a 'double negative' effect that adds a positive contribution to the overall spectral sensitivity of the circadian system.
findings.quote: The spectral sensitivity of circadian phototransduction would reflect this loss of inhibition by the rod mechanism as a positive addition to overall spectral sensitivity.
findings.empirical_support_cited: This plot provides indirect evidence that melatonin suppression begins near the level of rod bleaching and, thereby, that the net level of rod inhibition might progressively decline as more rhodopsin is bleached.

findings.antecedent: High light levels and radiation longer than ~500 nm (cross-point)
findings.mechanism: Under these conditions, the ipRGCs are free from rod inhibition and directly express their intrinsic photosensitivity (peak 480 nm) to the SCN.
findings.quote: At high light levels where cones are active and for radiation longer than the approximate 500-nm cross-point, the spectral response of the SCN is based upon the intrinsic photosensitive response of the ipRGC alone.

findings.antecedent: High light levels and radiation shorter than ~500 nm (cross-point)
findings.mechanism: The spectral response is a combination of the ipRGC's intrinsic response, the S cone bipolar's excitatory response, and the loss of shunting inhibition by rods (double negative).
findings.quote: At high light levels where cones are active and for radiation shorter than the cross-point, the spectral response of the SCN is modeled as a combination of the response from the ipRGC, the S cone (via the S cone bipolar), and the loss of shunting inhibition by rods.

findings.consequent: Spectral sensitivity functions for circadian response
findings.mechanism: The nonlinear characteristics of the model (rod inhibition, spectral opponency) mean that simple additivity does not hold, and spectral sensitivity varies with the spectral power distribution (SPD) of the source.
findings.quote: The model predicts that polychromatic light sources will have their own unique spectral sensitivity functions for a criterion level of circadian response.
findings.empirical_support_cited: The spectral opponency predicted by Eq. (1) also results in additivity failures.

findings.mechanism: The S cone bipolar provides a net depolarizing response that adds to the ipRGC response, leading to greater melatonin suppression at lower irradiances compared to white light.
findings.quote: The model predicts greater nocturnal melatonin suppression for the blue light than for the white light exposure.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Figueiro et al. [31] showed a surprising disparity between the flux densities needed to suppress human nocturnal melatonin after 1 h of exposures to narrow-band blue light (LED, λmax = 470 nm) and to polychromatic white light (mercury vapor).

findings.consequent: Signal from opponent S cone bipolar cell
findings.mechanism: White light, as a polychromatic source, produces no net depolarizing response from the S cone bipolar, meaning the circadian phototransduction is driven solely by the ipRGC's spectral sensitivity.
findings.quote: polychromatic white light, such as a mercury vapor light, would produce no signal from the opponent S cone bipolar cell.

testable_hypotheses_or_predictions: Rods set the threshold for circadian phototransduction, exemplified by nocturnal melatonin suppression.
The spectral sensitivity of the circadian system will vary from threshold to saturation with the spectral power distribution (SPD) of the light source.
Additivity failures for nocturnal melatonin suppression will be observed due to spectral opponency.
Polychromatic light sources will have unique spectral sensitivity functions for a given criterion level of circadian response.
Blue light will induce greater nocturnal melatonin suppression at lower irradiances compared to white light.
A sharp discontinuity in spectral sensitivity will be observed around 500 nm, representing the cross-point of the blue-yellow (b-y) system.
bridge_warrants: The model provides a framework for hypothesis testing and discussion of the practical aspects of architectural lighting with respect to light and health.
The model can be extended to accommodate new data and insights into human circadian phototransduction.

The model facilitates the discussion of architectural lighting applications for individuals with specific needs, such as seniors with Alzheimer's disease, premature infants in neonatal intensive care units, and shift workers.
The model helps to quantitatively frame the ongoing discussion about the impact of light at night (LAN) on circadian disruption.
methodological_critiques: Early psychophysical studies of circadian phototransduction often failed to properly specify the light stimulus, with spectral power distributions (SPDs) being unreported or modified by optical elements.
Previous studies often utilized constant flux densities to infer dose-response curves, assuming a linear system of phototransduction, which is inappropriate given nonlinear post-receptor processes.
model_structure: The model is a mathematical expression (Equation 1, with an alternative for rod saturation in Equation 2) that integrates the responses of ipRGCs, rods, and the b-y opponent signal. It includes parameters for sensitivity thresholds and signal strengths, and an exponential term for rod bleaching. A diode mathematical operator ensures that only depolarizing ON signals from the b-y system are added. The model is also represented by a neural circuit diagram (Fig. 1a) showing connections between rods, AII amacrine cells, A18 amacrine cells, S cone bipolars, and ipRGCs, and an electrical circuit representation (Fig. 1b).
limitations: The model is based largely upon human nocturnal melatonin suppression data, which is the most complete available for the purpose.

It assumes the model for human circadian phototransduction is equally useful for other outcome measures (e.g., phase shifting, core body temperature) as long as stimulus conditions are between threshold activation and response saturation.
The model assumes that the spectral sensitivity of the circadian system does not change with circadian time, despite some weak evidence suggesting otherwise.

The model does not address the wide range of responses generated by the circadian system to other aspects of the luminous stimulus, such as spatial distribution, timing and duration of exposure, and history of previous photic exposure.
The model does not incorporate cone or ipRGC saturation, as these phenomena likely occur at irradiances above those used to test nocturnal melatonin suppression.
The model is expected to be revised as more information on circadian phototransduction is acquired.
There are insufficient data to fully resolve the exact feature of gradual rod saturation via the A18 amacrine cell.
It is not known for certain whether circadian phototransduction leading to phase shifting and to nocturnal melatonin suppression are the same.

theory_commitments.theory_name: Model of Phototransduction by the Human Circadian System
theory_commitments.specific_claim: The paper proposes a comprehensive model detailing how light signals are detected by multiple photoreceptors (rods, cones, and intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells) in the human retina and subsequently integrated to drive the circadian system's responses, such as phase shifting and melatonin suppression.

mechanism_chain.description: Causal mechanism connecting light exposure to circadian responses via retinal phototransduction.

steps.from_construct: Environmental light (specific spectral composition, intensity, duration)

steps.to_construct: Generation of neural signals within the retina

steps.from_construct: Neural signals from multiple photoreceptors (integrated within the retina)
RHT input to the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN)
steps.to_construct: Modulation of SCN neuronal activity and clock gene expression
Regulation of circadian rhythms (e.g., melatonin secretion, sleep-wake cycle, alertness)
